analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health service giving free comprehensive health care to everyone, financed by new income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single hearing or vote: referred to nine House committees in August 1991, it sat in subcommittees and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, employer health insurance, and private practice with a single government-run U.S. Health Service. Every person in the country would get free comprehensive care — doctors, hospitals, dental, prescriptions, long-term care, mental health, and reproductive services — with no premiums or bills. It would be funded by a new income tax on individuals and corporations, end the tax break for employer health plans, and void employer obligations to provide health coverage. It also guarantees workers paid health leave, puts elected community boards in charge of facilities, and builds tuition-free health worker schools.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone in the United States who needs health care. The bill declares comprehensive health care a right for all residents, delivered without charge and without regard to income, race, age, or health status [S2][S3]. It covers prescription drugs, dental care, mental health, long-term care, abortion and contraception services, and eyeglasses and hearing aids [S2]. Workers gain a new right to paid leave for health care under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S2]. Existing health workers get a hiring guarantee, federal civil-service protections, and collective bargaining rights [S2]. Students in the new tuition-free health team schools get living-expense allowances and loan repayment in exchange for a service commitment [S2].

how_it_helps.text: All individuals within the United States would be eligible for free health care and supplemental services, with the Service barred from charging users or discriminating by income, race, age, or previous health status.

The Service must build a comprehensive health center in every community of roughly 25,000–50,000 people, a general hospital in every district, and a highly specialized regional facility — with a mandate to redistribute resources toward deprived inner-city and rural populations.

The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health insurance, and veterans' medical programs, replacing them all with the Service, and voids employer contractual obligations to provide health coverage.

The Service is financed through additional income taxes on individuals and corporations plus employer contributions, ending the tax exclusion for employer-paid medical premiums, and all existing Medicare trust fund assets are transferred to a new Health Service Trust Fund.

Health workers employed before enactment get hiring preference and a guarantee of appropriate employment in the Service, and Service employees keep federal civil service pay, benefits, and labor protections including binding arbitration.

Community health boards would be elected by local users and health workers, with public meetings, open records, recall elections, and grievance and legal-services programs to enforce patients' rights.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, individuals and corporations would pay an additional income tax calculated as a percentage of their normal tax, and the bill would end the income tax exclusion for employer-paid health premiums — so workers whose pay currently comes partly as untaxed health benefits would see that edge taxed. The private health insurance industry would lose its core business, private hospitals and doctors would be barred from delivering services in Service facilities after three years, and drug makers would face a national formulary, centralized purchasing, and possible government manufacturing. Employers would also have to fund workplace health facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Individuals and corporations via new income taxes

drawbacks.text: The financing is a substantial tax increase: a new additional income tax on individuals and corporations, the elimination of the tax exclusion for employer health contributions, and the repeal of existing medical expense deductions.

The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health coverage, and veterans' medical benefits on the effective date, so every current beneficiary's coverage would depend entirely on the new Service standing up community clinics, district hospitals, and regional facilities on schedule.

Three years after services begin, private delivery of health services in Service facilities is prohibited, and individuals employed by health boards are barred from private practice — a genuine restriction on doctors' professional freedom that supporters would have to defend.
The Service holds the power of eminent domain to condemn real estate, and students at the new health team schools must commit to two or more years of Service employment or owe damages.

The National Health Board would gain authority to issue debt obligations, with the Treasury required to purchase them in specified circumstances — an unusually powerful financing structure for an independent agency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is universal: no American would pay for care at the point of service, and the bill attacks the administrative overhead and unequal distribution it blames for the system's failures [S3]. The costs are equally real — a large tax increase, the deliberate elimination of private health insurance and fee-for-service practice, and the replacement of familiar programs like Medicare and Medicaid with a brand-new delivery system that would have to be built from scratch. Even a well-run transition would carry real risk for people who like their current coverage, and the bill's governance design — elected boards running hospitals and tuition-free schools with mandatory service — was far more ambitious than any health reform Congress has ever seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred jointly to nine House committees and scattered among their subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or markup, so it never came to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Dellums of California introduced the U.S. Health Service Act on August 2, 1991.

The same day, the House referred it jointly to nine committees: Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Banking, the District of Columbia, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Post Office and Civil Service, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means.
It was then referred to at least nine subcommittees across those committees, and executive comments were requested from OMB, OPM, and the Defense Department.

No further action of any kind was taken: the last recorded action is a subcommittee referral on April 23, 1992, and the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in the House or Senate before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
The bill had only one cosponsor, both sponsor and cosponsor being House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance industry, private hospitals and physician practices, and drug makers — all of whom the bill would have displaced — continued operating under the existing system unchanged, as did Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the existing system

against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer and government-run health restructuring nationally during this period, a campaign a well-informed reader would recognize from the era's health reform fights.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so opposition was never recorded; support came entirely from two House Democrats — Dellums and one cosponsor — with no Republican involvement.

industries.note: The bill voids employer health coverage obligations, repeals federal programs that pay private insurers, and bars issuers of health insurance policies from serving on health boards — effectively ending private health insurance as the delivery channel. Its disappearance would have removed premiums, deductibles, and claim denials from ordinary people's lives.

All care would be delivered by salaried Service workers in Service facilities; three years after startup, private delivery in Service facilities is banned and board employees may not practice privately. Fee-for-service practice would end.

A National Pharmacy and Medical Supply Formulary would set what drugs are covered, regional boards would centrally purchase and distribute drugs, and the National Board could build its own manufacturing facilities if needed.

Employers would owe new income taxes and workplace health facilities, but their contractual obligations to pay for employee and retiree health care would be voided — trading a large recurring liability for a tax bill.
Existing health worker education programs would be phased into tuition-free Service-funded health team schools with student stipends, and students would owe a multi-year service commitment in return.
